newsitem.title: USA: Fergie finds fans and fortune in United States.
newsitem.headline: Fergie finds fans and fortune in United States.

text.p: What is a flame-haired, formerly fat, formerly married British royal to do when she is in debt, rejected and ridiculed at home?
For the Duchess of York the answer was to go West to find fame, fortune and even fans in a former British colony.

The United States, which prides itself on welcoming immigrants and laying down the red carpet for rubbished royalty, even British royalty, was treating the former Sarah Ferguson with the sort of respect she had not had for more than a decade at home -- the first years of her marriage to Britain's Prince Andrew when she was fondly called "Great Fun Fergie."

In the space of a week in the United States, Fergie signed high-priced deals to hawk cranberry juice on television and be a spokeswoman for Weight Watchers International, the programme she credited for helping her slim down several times and shed her "Duchess of Pork" image.
The only sour note of the week came when the Los Angeles designer Mr Blackwell named her to his 10 worst dressed list, saying she resembled "an unemployed barmaid in search of a crown."

The TV ad and Weight Watchers deals were on top of a reported $2 million she received for her memoirs, a slim, swiftly written "mea culpa" called "My Story," that topped U.S. bestseller lists through Christmas, selling more than 500,000 copies and leaving its once-nervous publisher relieved and delighted.

The British press, which hammers Fergie every chance it gets, which is often daily, savaged her book, slammed her ad deal as breaking royal tradition and gave short-shrift to her embrace of Weight Watchers.
It was the sort of treatment the Duchess has often said she has come to expect from the British press.

"The media once dubbed me 'Great Fun Fergie,' saying 'She's a breath of Fresh Air,' then it was 'Round Fergie,' then 'Fat Fergie,' which gave way to 'Fat and Appalling Fergie' and then ultimately, my favourite, 'the Duchess of Pork,'" she told reporters at a Weight Watchers news conference.

Later, a passing reference by the Duchess in a newspaper interview to putting her 8-year-old daughter, Princess Beatrice, on a diet led to a new attack from the tabloid newspapers of London's Fleet Street, which found experts declaring children should never diet because that could cause anorexia.

"She is like the British Tonya Harding," says People magazine associate editor Janice Min, referring to the U.S. ice skater who thought the best way to go to the Olympics was having an aide bash her opponent's knee with a metal bar.

Min said that while the Duchess of York may be hated at home, she was doing fine in the United States because "America is a land of opportunity, where basically all you have to do to be forgiven is say you're sorry, which the duchess did."

She added Ferguson was also successful because "a lot of women can relate to her. She got into a foolish marriage, eats too much, dresses really badly and is typical of our worst anxieties about ourselves, and she did the ultimate thing, penned a 'tell-all.'"

Adweek columnist Barbara Lippert took a different view of Fergie's new-found success. "We are seeing the work of Howard Rubenstein as her P.R. man and deal-maker. If he can change the image of Leona Helmsley and other felons, he can do glamour deals for the duchess."
But even Lippert admitted, "There is something we like about the renegade who is overweight and who doesn't fit in."
Rubenstein, a prominent New York city public relations man, denied that he had such power.
He said the duchess was received with great warmth in the United States "because people are ready to accept her apology for what she has done in the past.

"In England she has had many years of negative press. I firmly believe that after they see she is a hard-working woman who gives great love to her children, the media there will turn around and be as fair to her as the media in the United States is."
